column2: Diamante! A Stone from the Orange River

A bright stone found near Hopetown has passed from a riverbank household to traders and examiners. The Eureka diamond is small enough to rest in a hand, yet its identification has unsettled every assumption about the value of this frontier. Reports travel by wagon and newspaper, encouraging men to search the gravels of the Orange and Vaal. The first find is not the great Kimberley mine: that transformation still lies ahead. For now, scattered diggings, uncertain claims and the expense of supplies shape a precarious new livelihood. The surrounding district is beginning to supply and organise these early workings. Farmers can sell food and draught animals, merchants can extend credit, and newcomers can stake claims, but Griqua landholders and African communities also have rights at stake. We must decide whether to establish a public claims office with surveyed boundaries and recorded agreements, or allow private diggers to organise the first rush themselves.
The Dry Diggings: A City of Diamonds

The Star of South Africa discovery in 1869 helped turn rumours into a determined search. Now the rich dry diggings around Vooruitzigt and Colesberg Kopje have drawn the rush away from scattered river gravels toward concentrated deposits beneath the earth. Tents, claims, stores and wagon tracks crowd together where a mining town is taking shape. The settlement will become Kimberley, but its wealth does not settle the competing claims of Griqua authorities, the Boer republics and Britain. Thousands of newcomers require water, food, timber and transport. African workers join the expanding labour market while small diggers struggle with boundaries, collapsing workings and the growing cost of extraction. The province's mining economy is entering a larger phase, and the renewed boom will attract people and investment. A properly staffed claims office can improve production and record obligations, while privately organised diggings offer a cheaper, less orderly route to rapid expansion.
Goud aan die Ooskus! The Andriesburg Discoveries

Republican surveyors and local prospectors have returned to Andriesburg with samples that survive repeated washing and assay. Reports of payable gold in the district's hinterland are bringing a new urgency to the eastern settlement. Coastal access offers a practical advantage: equipment and provisions can arrive by sea before travelling inland to the workings, while merchants see opportunities in freight, storage and credit. The volksraad's eastern venture now promises more than an outlet for inland trade, but its officers warn that a new field must be proved claim by claim. A promising sample does not build a road, settle a land dispute or secure safe water for a camp. Local communities, labourers, claimholders and officials all have interests in the new field. A funded survey and registration service would give the rush a firmer basis, while private enterprise could open the workings immediately at less cost to the treasury.
Goud! The Reefs of the Witwatersrand

Payable gold has been identified along the Witwatersrand, and reports from the Main Reef are drawing prospectors toward the ridge. The outcrops promise something different from a brief river-gravel rush: a mineral belt whose extraction will demand machinery, capital and organised labour. Johannesburg is taking shape among farms, camps and surveyed claims. Wagons bring food and equipment, traders open stores, and newcomers arrive with skills and ambitions that will change the balance of the old pastoral republic. African workers are central to the emerging mines, even as land and labour arrangements place them under growing pressure. The first workings can be opened with modest equipment, but deeper ore will require sustained investment and new technical solutions. Mineral revenue offers the government roads, services and financial strength, while also raising difficult questions about foreign investment and political rights. We can fund a registration service and survey the field, or let private diggers lead the opening of the Rand.
A diamond rush draws newcomers and expands the local mining population.
